content.title: About
content.content: Enoki (Flammulina velutipes) are thin, white, crunchy mushrooms with long, slender stems. Native to East Asia, they are traditionally used in soups, salads, and noodle dishes. Enoki have a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a characteristic crisp “snap” when bitten.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Enoki are often called “tree mushrooms” because of their dense, woody texture.
In Japan they are cultivated in dark, cool rooms where the temperature is kept around 5 °C.
The fungi can convert wood waste into edible biomass, making them an environmentally sustainable food.
Enoki are rich in polysaccharides that may support the immune system.
Traditional Chinese medicine uses enoki as a tonic for liver and kidney health.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Enoki provide niacin, riboflavin, and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: One cup of fresh enoki (~70 g) supplies about 2 g of protein with very few calories.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polysaccharides and ergothioneine in enoki help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in these mushrooms promotes a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Enoki are naturally low in salt, making them suitable for low‑sodium diets.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to enoki, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Mushrooms contain purines, so people with gout should limit intake.

items.title: Needs cooking
items.content: Raw enoki can be hard to digest; a brief boil or sauté is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add enoki to soups, broths, ramen, salads, or quickly stir‑fry them with vegetables. They are often used as a garnish for rice or noodles. Before cooking, rinse and pat the mushrooms dry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store enoki in the refrigerator in a loosely sealed bag; they stay fresh for 5–7 days. For longer storage, blanch them for 2–3 minutes and freeze.
